## Final Output

Everyone converged on the same shape for this app, with no real fights left standing.

**What it is:** Not just a Pomodoro clone — the goal is to feel like a quiet coach that manages the work/break rhythm for you, not a stopwatch you have to babysit. Open the app, hit Start in under 2 seconds, and trust it to auto-advance through work → break → work and track the cycle count.

**Screen structure:** One screen, no tab bar, no nav stack. The circular timer is the entire home screen. Settings (gear icon) and History (list icon) are auxiliary — presented as sheets, not separate tabs — so the ring is always the very first thing you see.

**The backgrounding/timer-accuracy fix (this was the key technical risk raised, and everyone agreed on the same fix):** Don't decrement a stored "seconds remaining" counter. Instead store an absolute start timestamp + target duration, and always recompute remaining time as `target - Date().timeIntervalSince(start)` on appear / scenePhase changes. This means if the user backgrounds the app and comes back after the session would've ended, the app correctly shows it as already complete and already auto-advanced — not a countdown frozen or "catching up."

**Force-quit / app-kill behavior:** Treated as an accepted, named limitation rather than something to engineer around. If the user force-quits mid-session, the app resets to the start of the current mode on relaunch — no attempt at reconciling "what did I miss," no persisted in-progress state. Simple and honest, not silently lying about progress.

**History:** Flat, reverse-chronological list, one SwiftData model, no grouping/charts/streaks/delete. Append-only, and only on **natural completion** (timer hits zero and auto-advances) — hitting Reset logs nothing, since the point of history is to be a truthful record of what was actually stuck with. Every mode (work, short break, long break) gets logged the same way.

**Reset behavior, locked down:** Reset only restarts the *current* interval back to full duration — it does not touch the cycle count and does not jump to a different mode. There's no skip-forward button in this build; that's explicitly called out as a real gap but intentionally left for V2 rather than half-building it.

**Polish guardrails:** Standard SwiftUI animation primitives for the ring — no custom Bezier paths, to avoid last-minute debugging risk.

No open disagreements remain — Gemini's "reset to start of current mode on force-quit" was just making concrete what Claude had already flagged as an accepted limitation, not a contested point.

## Final Output

Everyone landed in the same place, so here's the locked design for this sprint.

**Screen structure:** One screen only — the circular timer fills the home screen, no tab bar, no navigation stack. Settings (gear icon) and History (list icon) are presented as sheets that slide up and away. Nothing gets promoted to a full destination.

**Timer state model:** Timestamp-based, not a ticking counter. State is `phase + startDate + duration`, plus minimal pause bookkeeping (a `pausedAt` folded back in on resume). The UI is a pure projection of that state — recomputed on appear and on `scenePhase` changes, never mutated tick-by-tick.

**Reconciliation on resume — capped at exactly one phase transition.** If the current phase has elapsed, complete and log that one phase, advance to the next, and start its clock from "now." Never cascade through multiple auto-completions no matter how long the app was backgrounded. This is a hard design rule, not an implementation detail — it's what keeps history truthful and stops someone from "cleaning it up" into a while-loop later.

**History:** Flat, reverse-chronological, one SwiftData model. Logged only on natural completion (including the single reconciled transition above). Resets, backgrounding, and force-quit relaunches log nothing. Force-quit mid-session resets to the start of the current phase on relaunch — an accepted, named limitation, not something we engineer around.

**Main-screen polish, kept intentionally small:**
- A one-line "Work 2 of 4" style label near the ring, bound to existing cycle-count + sessions-before-long-break state. This is the entire concession to "quiet coach" — no charts, no streaks, no per-day summaries.
- A soft, standard SwiftUI scale-and-fade on the ring when a resume detects a completed phase transition, so the jump doesn't feel jarring.
- Two distinct haptic patterns, fired only at phase start and phase completion — nothing on pause, nothing on reset. Hold this line strictly; it's explicitly scoped in the prompt and anything more is unscoped polish we don't have time for.

**Settings:** A plain `Form` with `Stepper` rows for the three durations plus one integer `Stepper` for sessions-before-long-break (default 4). No custom pickers, no presets UI.

**Reset:** Restarts only the current interval to full duration. Doesn't touch cycle count, doesn't change phase, logs nothing. No skip-forward control in this build — that's a known, deliberate gap for V2.

This carries forward as the spec for the next phase to build against.

Alright, everyone's converged and the one real correction on the table — the `completedAt` timestamp bug — has no dissent, so I'm locking this in.

CONSENSUS: YES

## Final Output

**State machine:** One source of truth, no ticking counter. `TimerEngine` is an `@Observable` class holding `phase` (`.work`/`.shortBreak`/`.longBreak`), `phaseStartedAt`, `phaseDuration`, `isPaused`, `pausedAt`, plus `completedWorkSessions` (cycle count) and the configured durations/sessions-before-long-break. Remaining time is always computed, never stored: `phaseDuration - Date().timeIntervalSince(phaseStartedAt)` (adjusted for pause time folded back in on resume). Instantiated once at the App root, injected via `.environment`. It's the sole owner of: computing remaining time, deciding phase transitions, writing to SwiftData, and firing haptics. Settings and History are pure readers/writers of engine state — no timer or persistence logic anywhere else.

**Public contract (write this file first, before any lane forks):**
```
start()      // begin current phase from now
pause()      // record pausedAt
resume()     // fold paused duration back into phaseStartedAt
reset()      // restart current phase at full duration; no log, no phase/cycle change
reconcile()  // called on appear + scenePhase → .active
```
`reconcile()` is capped at exactly one phase transition, no matter how long the app was backgrounded — if elapsed time crosses multiple boundaries, complete and log the current phase, advance one step, start the new phase's clock from now, and stop. This is a hard rule enforced by the implementation (guard against a while-loop), not just a convention.

**Timestamp fix (the one real correction this round):** When `reconcile()` detects a completed phase, log it with `completedAt = phaseStartedAt + phaseDuration` — the moment the phase actually finished — never `Date()` at resume time. Likewise `durationSeconds` in the log is always the configured/planned duration, never measured wall-clock elapsed. History reflects when things actually finished and how long they were meant to run, not when the user happened to reopen the app.

**Data model:** One flat SwiftData model, `SessionEntry`: `completedAt: Date`, `mode: Mode` (enum: work/shortBreak/longBreak), `durationSeconds: Int`. No relationships, no extra fields. Only `TimerEngine` touches the `ModelContext` for writes; `History` view only reads. Logged only on natural completion (including the single reconciled transition) — never on reset, pause, or plain backgrounding.

**Haptics:** Two patterns — phase start, phase completion — fired from inside the engine's transition logic (`start()`/`reconcile()`), never from button tap handlers directly, so a completion that happens during a background reconcile still fires the haptic exactly once when the app resumes.

**Testability:** The engine takes its time source as an injectable dependency (defaults to `Date()`, but overridable in tests) so reconciliation math can be unit tested deterministically: exact-zero completion, partial elapsed resume, multi-boundary resume (verifying single-step advance), and reset-logs-nothing.

**Timer tick:** Single `Timer.publish(every: 1, on: .main, in: .common)`, invalidated on pause and on background, restarted only through the `scenePhase`-triggered `reconcile()` path. No `TimelineView(.animation)`.

**Build lanes (engine contract ships first, then parallel):**
1. `TimerEngine` + reconciliation logic + ring UI (owns the app shell's `scenePhase` observer too — this is the engine's only caller, not a separate concern)
2. SwiftData `SessionEntry` + History sheet (read-only)
3. Settings sheet (Form + Steppers, mutates engine's duration config)

Lane 1 must land the engine's public surface (the five methods above) as a locked contract before 2 and 3 write code against it.

## Final Output

FocusFlow is done — a one-screen Pomodoro timer with the circular countdown ring, Start/Pause/Reset, auto-advancing work → short break → long break cycle tracking, a Settings sheet for durations, and a History sheet backed by SwiftData. Everything the three lanes built now fits together as one coherent app:

- **`TimerEngine`** (Core) is the single source of truth — timestamp-based, never a ticking counter, with reconciliation capped at exactly one phase transition and truthful `completedAt` logging tied to when a phase actually finished, not when the app happened to be reopened.
- **`ContentView`/`TimerRingView`** (Frontend) drive the visible per-second tick via an explicitly connected/disconnected `Timer.publish`, since `@Observable` alone won't repaint on wall-clock time passing. The Start button correctly routes fresh phases through `engine.start()` (so the phase-start haptic fires and a just-changed Settings duration takes effect) versus `engine.resume()` for a genuinely paused mid-phase timer.
- **`SettingsView`/`HistoryView`/`HapticManager`** (Backend) are all wired: Settings mutates the engine's live config through `Stepper`s, History is a real `@Query` off SwiftData (no more placeholder), and haptics fire from inside the engine's transition logic so a background-reconciled completion still buzzes once on resume.
- **`FocusFlowApp`** (the entry point, mine to own) builds the `ModelContainer` for `SessionEntry`, constructs `TimerEngine` with a real `SwiftDataSessionEntryRecorder`, and injects the engine via `.environment()` — this was already correctly done from the prior round, I just verified it end to end.

I checked the whole tree for the two things that would've silently broken a build — duplicate type/protocol declarations and stale TODO stubs — and found none; the bugs flagged in earlier rounds (duplicate `Mode.displayName`, `remainingTime` vs `remainingTimeInterval` mismatch, missing tick timer, `reset()` silently unpausing, HistoryView's SwiftData stub) are all resolved in the files on disk.

The one integration gap I found and fixed myself: `project.yml` had no code-signing settings, which would've blocked even a plain simulator build via `xcodegen generate && xcodebuild`. Added `CODE_SIGN_STYLE: Automatic` / `CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED: NO` / `CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED: NO` so it builds and runs in the simulator with no dev team required (real-device signing is legitimately out of scope for a local-only demo).

**Honest gap:** I could not actually run `xcodegen generate` / `xcodebuild` in this sandbox — those commands hit an approval wall in this non-interactive session (same limitation Codex and Claude both hit in earlier rounds). Everything above is verified by careful manual reading of every file for type/contract consistency, not a compiler. **To run it:** from `app_build/`, run `xcodegen generate`, open `FocusFlow.xcodeproj`, and build/run the `FocusFlow` scheme on an iOS 17+ simulator — that first real compiler pass is the one thing nobody in this sprint has been able to do yet, so it's worth doing before calling this fully shippable.

**Build verification:** build left unverified (no .xcodeproj/.xcworkspace found.)

## Final Output

The call is a **conditional go**, not a clean go and not a no-go: the design and code are sound, but nobody has ever actually run this app, and that's the one thing that has to happen before anyone says "shipped."

**What's locked and not up for re-debate:** the timestamp-based `TimerEngine`, single-phase-transition reconciliation, truthful `completedAt` logging tied to when a phase actually finished, and treating force-quit as a clean cold-start rather than something to reconcile — all correct, all done, no notes.

**The one blocking gap:** three build lanes have each independently verified this "by careful static read," and each round caught real bugs that way (duplicate `displayName`, `remainingTime` mismatch, `reset()` silently unpausing). That's proof the method works, but also proof it has limits — a compiler has never once touched this code. That stops being a code risk and becomes a process fact: this app is code-complete with zero compiler passes.

**What the human needs to do before calling this shippable** — five minutes, not more static analysis:
1. `cd app_build && xcodegen generate`, open `FocusFlow.xcodeproj`, run the `FocusFlow` scheme on an iOS 17+ simulator.
2. Walk this exact six-item checklist:
   - App launches, ring animates
   - Start / Pause / Reset all work
   - One natural completion writes exactly one history row
   - A Settings duration change takes effect next phase
   - Backgrounding and returning mid-phase reconciles exactly one phase transition, never a cascade
   - Force-quit relaunch shows a clean, full-duration current phase — no one-frame flash of stale state (grep `TimerEngine` for any `UserDefaults`/`AppStorage` rehydration of live phase state as a quick sanity check; it should init fresh every cold launch)
3. If anything fails, it's a bug fix against a known-sound architecture, not a redesign.

**One small copy fix to make before/at that pass, if not already done:** rename the History sheet's title to "Completed Sessions" and give its empty state text like "Sessions you finish will show up here" — this heads off the confusion of a user who resets repeatedly and wonders where their activity went, since the history model is deliberately append-only-on-completion.

That's the whole final-review verdict: architecture and scope are settled and correct, the deliverable is code-complete pending exactly one human simulator pass against the checklist above, and that pass — not another round of reading — is what turns this from "should work" into "works."
